title: Principles of Effective Prison Work
author: Harry Fletcher-Wood
summary: Harry Fletcher-Wood, writing about the Leading Prison Landings project, lays out four principles behind effective prison officer work: prisoners must experience procedural justice, officers should treat every moment as a rehabilitative opportunity, officers must be warm while maintaining firm boundaries, and discretion must be applied consistently across individuals. He grounds each principle in research and practitioner testimony from prison studies literature, showing how the same underlying dynamics -- being explicit about the reasoning behind a decision, using brief interactions as micro-moments of encouragement, balancing openness with appropriate limits, and applying "like cases alike" -- determine whether authority is experienced as fair or arbitrary. The piece is the first in a series; a follow-up will cover 24 specific strategies built on these four principles.
points: Fletcher-Wood's procedural justice principle distinguishes between an objectively fair outcome and one perceived as fair -- the same sanction lands differently depending on whether an officer explains the reasoning or simply asserts authority.

His "every moment as rehabilitation" principle reframes routine tasks (locking doors, roll call) as accumulating opportunities for brief, encouraging interventions rather than pure compliance-checking.

The warmth-and-boundaries principle uses a small example -- how an officer answers "where are you from?" -- to show how relationship-building and appropriate limits trade off against each other in daily interactions.

On discretion, Fletcher-Wood argues it is simultaneously necessary (no rulebook covers every situation) and risky (today's exception becomes tomorrow's expectation), resolved only by officers consistently treating like cases alike.
quotes: Effective prison work means making a series of choices under pressure – officers select, adapt, and switch strategies to achieve their goals.
Procedural justice means that decisions are made in ways that are visibly fair. To achieve this, prisoners must know why and how a decision was made, and what informed it.

A transformative prison officer will look to use the momentary interaction as they lock prisoners away as a chance to help prisoners rethink their actions, choose fresh goals, commit to change, and act on their commitments.
We combine clear, firm boundaries with a warm, caring approach. Firm boundaries are crucial in keeping the prison safe, maintaining consistent rules, and helping prisoners behave appropriately.
Whenever discretion is exercised, the risk is that an exception today becomes an expectation tomorrow.
The more officers can be consistent in the way they meet individuals’ needs, the clearer expectations are for prisoners and officers alike.
